Acquisition: first colony, an offered discovery, enough owls and your turn. Cost = round up (100 × (acquired discoveries + 1) × difficulty factor). Excess owls remain. Each discovery is acquired once; effects apply across your civilisation. One-time effects do not repeat. Difficulty factors: Discoverer 0.75; Explorer 0.90; Conquistador 1; Governor 1.15; Viceroy 1.30. No prerequisite discovery is required.
The Athenian Treasury held offerings and spoils dedicated to Apollo. Its surviving, reassembled facade connects victory, wealth and sanctuary.
A marble fragment from the Athenian Acropolis depicts trireme rowers. It records the organisation of Greek naval warfare; the sea raider bonus is a thematic association.
The surviving hull of a Greek merchant ship from the late fourth century BC reveals ancient shipbuilding. The reference is a merchant vessel; the game reward remains a warship.
The bronze Corinthian helmet protected a Greek warrior’s head, nose and cheeks. Its profile shows the characteristic nose and cheek guards.
A bronze helmet dedicated at Olympia bears Miltiades’ name. It is surviving evidence of a military dedication; unit promotion is a thematic interpretation.
An Athenian stele of 337/336 BC carries a law against tyranny. Its relief shows Democracy crowning Demos, the personified people.
Greek cities displayed agreements on stone stelae. An alliance decree in the Acropolis Museum is the reference; the simplified handshake symbolises agreement.
Terracotta water clocks measured speakers’ allotted time in Athenian courts. Escaping water provided a measure of speaking time.
Stone lists recorded the portion of allied tribute dedicated to Athena. They document the administration of the Athenian-led league’s revenues.
Surviving Athenian decrees record citizenship grants and honours to individuals. In the game they symbolise acceptance and cooperation, not historical universal equality.
Votive plaques from Penteskouphia near Corinth depict potters and the firing of vessels. The kiln scene is a simplified interpretation of these surviving images.
Athenian mortgage markers identified property encumbered by an obligation. A marker does not prove a particular cancellation; the game’s debt relief is a thematic interpretation.
Boundary stones marked the limits of the Athenian Agora. The defined boundary symbolises a land-use agreement, not a historical right of free appropriation.
Rhodian amphorae carried stamps recording production and officials. The selected circular impression uses the rose emblem of Rhodes.
The cargo and hull of the Kyrenia ship document Mediterranean trade. Voyages linked ports and carried goods and news; the game’s power report is a stylisation.
Two hymns carved in stone at Delphi preserve Greek text and musical notation. They are exceptional evidence of ancient religious music.
A surviving Cyrene stele records Theran civic rights and an oath associated with the city’s foundation. The inscription is later than the founding expedition itself.
Delphic inscriptions record the release of enslaved people through formal sale to Apollo. Historical freedom and citizenship were not the same status.
A Corinthian terracotta figure carries a torch and piglet, attributes associated with Demeter and Persephone. Whether it represents a goddess or a worshipper is uncertain.
The Hellenistic victory goddess stands on a ship-prow pedestal. She survives without head or arms; the conversion bonus is game symbolism.
Greek gold wreaths imitate plant twigs and leaves. Surviving examples evoke honours and social ties; the link to the game’s register of cities is a loose symbolic association.
Plaque F 871 from Penteskouphia is a surviving Greek depiction of pottery-clay extraction. The drawing translates its work scene into a simplified game illustration.
Messene preserves extensive stone fortifications with towers and gates. They symbolise organised defence for the game’s stockade, rather than its building material.
The surviving bronze gearing calculated astronomical and calendar cycles. It is not an established shipboard navigation instrument; the sailing bonus represents astronomical knowledge more broadly.
The carved stone represents the mythical navel of the world and is associated with Apollo’s oracle at Delphi. In the game it symbolises foresight; protection of explorers is fictional.
The ship arrives in Home port before independence. After independence it needs a safe coastal colony; delivery waits if none is available. The reward is granted only once.
Unlocked buildings still require their usual population, prerequisite buildings and construction resources.
